title: Glaucus
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 8719b7d375018d4f. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Galatea has finished her story, and the Nereids scatter into the calm water. Scylla, wandering the shore without her clothes, is seen by Glaucus — lately changed from a man into a creature of the deep — and runs in fear to the top of a hill near the sea, where she is safe and cannot tell whether he is a monster or a god. Leaning on the rock that stood nearest, he tells her how he was a fisherman, how a strange grass sent his own catch flopping back into the water and then drew him in after it, and how the sea-gods washed his mortality out of him; he ends by asking what any of it is worth if it does not touch her, and Scylla walks away while he is still talking, leaving him to make for the halls of Circe in a rage.

sentences.t:
Desierat Galatea loqui, coetuque soluto
discedunt placidisque natant Nereides undis.
sentences.l: Galatea had ceased to speak, and, the gathering broken up, they separate and the Nereids swim in calm waters.
sentences.i: Galatea had finished speaking; the company broke up, and the Nereids went off swimming through the quiet water.
sentences.n: The pluperfect desierat looks back: Galatea had been talking, and by the time this line opens she has stopped. coetu soluto is an ablative absolute: a noun and a participle in the ablative, standing outside the sentence's own grammar, where English wants a whole clause — “once the gathering had broken up”. It is worth recognising on sight, because it comes back three more times in these lines (905, 936, 952). In 899 the adjective placidis and its noun undis are pulled apart to enclose the verb and its subject, natant Nereides.

sentences.t:
Scylla redit (neque enim medio se credere ponto
audet) et aut bibula sine vestibus errat harena,
aut, ubi lassata est, seductos nacta recessus
gurgitis, inclusa sua membra refrigerat unda.
sentences.l: Scylla returns (for she does not dare to trust herself to the mid-sea) and either roams without her clothes on the thirsty sand, or, when she has grown tired, having found the secluded recesses of the pool, cools her limbs in the shut-in water.
sentences.i: Scylla comes back — she will not trust herself to the open sea — and either wanders naked along the thirsty sand, or, when she has tired of that, finds some out-of-the-way pool and cools her body in its shut-in water.
sentences.n: The parenthesis is the edition's own. credere takes a dative: se credere ponto is “to entrust herself to the sea”. nacta is the perfect participle of the deponent nanciscor, so it is passive in form but active in sense — “having found”, not “having been found”; the same trick returns with lapsi at 954. bibula harena and inclusa unda are both ablatives of place. sine vestibus is plain and unhedged, and it stands in the first of the two alternatives, with errat harena: she is wandering the sand with nothing on. The poem says it before Glaucus arrives, which is what gives her flight at 908 its force.

sentences.t:
Ecce fretum scindens alti novus incola ponti,
nuper in Euboica versis Anthedone membris,
sentences.l: Behold, cleaving the strait, a new dweller of the deep sea, his limbs lately turned in Euboean Anthedon,
sentences.i: And look — cutting through the water, a newcomer to the deep, his body only lately transformed at Anthedon on the Euboean strait —
sentences.n: Two lines of description arrive before the subject has a name: Glaucus is held back to the first word of 906. novus incola ponti, “a new dweller of the deep”, says both that he has recently arrived and that he was not born to it. versis membris is another ablative absolute, like coetu soluto at 898. Anthedon is a coastal town facing Euboea across the strait, so Euboica locates it rather than moving it. Magnus prints scindens, “cleaving”; some editions print stringens, “grazing, skimming”, which has him brush the surface rather than split it.

sentences.l: Glaucus is there, and is held fast by desire for the girl he has seen, and whatever words he thinks can delay her as she flees, he brings out.
sentences.i: Glaucus is there; the sight of the girl holds him fixed with desire, and he pours out every word he thinks might slow her down as she flees.
sentences.n: visae virginis is an objective genitive with cupidine — the desire is directed at the girl, and visae, “seen”, makes the sight of her its cause. haeret is “sticks fast”: he stops dead where he is. The object of refert is quaecumque … verba, and the two halves are split across the line-end, quaecumque in 907 and verba first in 908, with the indirect statement putat [verba] posse morari fugientem standing between them. fugientem is accusative and stands for Scylla — the participle has the same form for masculine and feminine, and only the context makes it her — and its tense matters: she is already in flight before he has said a word.

sentences.t:
fugit illa tamen veloxque timore
pervenit in summum positi prope litora montis.
sentences.l: she flees nevertheless, and, swift from fear, reaches the top of a mountain set near the shore.
sentences.i: She flees all the same; fear makes her fast, and she reaches the summit of a mountain standing close to the shore.
sentences.n: fugit here is present, not perfect. Scanning 908 foot by foot: ver-ba-re / fert-fu-git / il-la-ta / men-ve / lox-que-ti / mo-re, that is dactyl, dactyl, dactyl, spondee, dactyl, spondee — sixteen syllables. The second foot needs both syllables of fugit short, as in the present fŭgĭt; the perfect fūgit would make the first syllable heavy and leave the light -git to open the third foot, which no foot can do. The present keeps her flight in the same tense as refert just before it. summum … montis is a neuter adjective doing a noun's work with a genitive under it, “the top of the mountain”, and positi prope litora is a participle phrase inside that genitive.

sentences.t:
Ante fretum est ingens, apicem conlectus in unum,
longa sub arboribus convexus in aequora vertex:
sentences.l: In front of the strait there is a huge peak, gathered into a single point, arched out beneath its trees over the long waters:
sentences.i: Facing the water there stands a great height, drawn together to one point, tree-covered, bending out over the open sea:
sentences.n: The noun vertex is the last word of 911, after three things have already been said about it: ingens, then conlectus in unum apicem, then convexus. conlectus is the perfect participle of conligo used as a bare adjective, “drawn together”. In 911 longa and its noun aequora are pulled apart with sub arboribus convexus between them. The colon at the end is the edition's, and it points forward: the sentence it introduces is what Scylla does on this peak.

sentences.t:
constitit hic, et tuta loco, monstrumne deusne
ille sit, ignorans, admiraturque colorem
caesariemque umeros subiectaque terga tegentem,
ultimaque excipiat quod tortilis inguina piscis.
sentences.l: She halted here, and, safe by the place, not knowing whether he is a monster or a god, she marvels at his colour and at his hair covering his shoulders and the back set beneath them, and that a twisting fish takes up his lowest groin.
sentences.i: She stopped there. Safe where she stood, and unable to tell whether he was a monster or a god, she stared at his colour, at the hair covering his shoulders and the back under it, and at the way a coiling fish took over below his groin.
sentences.n: constitit is perfect and admiratur is present: the historic present takes over the moment she begins to look, and this alternation of perfect and present runs on through the part. tuta loco is an ablative of cause — the position is what makes her safe. monstrumne deusne ille sit is a double indirect question (-ne … -ne, “whether … or”) with the subjunctive sit, governed by ignorans. tegentem is accusative singular and agrees with caesariem alone, though the hair covers both umeros and terga. admiratur then changes construction and takes a quod-clause with the subjunctive excipiat, so she wonders at a fact as well as at objects; excipio is the verb for one thing taking over where another leaves off.

sentences.t:
Sensit et innitens, quae stabat proxima, moli,
“non ego prodigium nec sum fera belua, virgo,
sed deus” inquit “aquae:
sentences.l: He perceived it, and, leaning on a rock-mass, the one that stood nearest, “I am not a portent, nor am I a wild beast, girl, but a god,” he says, “of the water:
sentences.i: He saw what she was thinking, and, leaning on the nearest rock, said: “I am no portent, girl, and no wild animal, but a god of the water:
sentences.n: sensit has no expressed object: what he takes in is the doubt and the staring just described. innitens governs the dative moli, and the relative clause quae stabat proxima is wedged in front of that noun, so moli lands last in 916. The edition sets inquit between deus and its genitive aquae, so the claim reaches Scylla in two pieces — the same breaking of quoted words around an intruding word happens again at 942 and 947. prodigium is an unnatural thing, a portent; belua is a brute. He is answering her doubt of 912–913 in her own terms, though he swaps her monstrum for prodigium and belua.

sentences.t:
nec maius in aequore Proteus
ius habet et Triton Athamantiadesque Palaemon.
sentences.l: nor has Proteus greater right in the sea, and Triton and Palaemon, son of Athamas.
sentences.i: Proteus holds no greater authority in the sea than I do, and neither do Triton or Palaemon, Athamas' son.
sentences.n: ius is the word for legal standing, jurisdiction — title rather than raw power — and maius ius makes the boast a claim to equality with these three, not superiority over them. habet is singular, fixed by the nearest subject Proteus, with the two further subjects added after it. Athamantiades is a Greek-style patronymic, “son of Athamas”, and the edition keeps the Greek shape of the word. Magnus prints in aequore, ablative, “in the sea”; the other witness reads in aequora, accusative.

sentences.t:
Ante tamen mortalis eram, sed, scilicet altis
deditus aequoribus, tantum exercebar in illis.
sentences.l: Before, however, I was mortal, but, given over of course to the deep waters, I busied myself only in them.
sentences.i: I was mortal before all this; but I was a man given to the deep, and I worked nowhere but there.
sentences.n: deditus takes the dative altis aequoribus. exercebar is passive in form but middle in sense — “I kept myself busy”, not “I was worked by somebody”. scilicet is a conversational aside, “of course”, as though the point needed no arguing. Magnus prints deditus, “given over”, and tantum, “only”; the other witness reads debitus, “owed, already promised”, and iam tum, “even then” — a text in which the sea has a claim on him long before he eats the grass.

sentences.t:
Nam modo ducebam ducentia retia pisces,
nunc in mole sedens moderabar harundine linum.
sentences.l: For at one time I was drawing nets that were drawing fish, at another, sitting on a rock-mass, I was working the line with a reed.
sentences.i: Sometimes I hauled in nets that were hauling in fish; sometimes I sat out on the rocks and played a line on a rod.
sentences.n: modo … nunc is “at one time … at another”; nunc here is not “now”. ducebam ducentia puts the same verb into the man and into his nets inside one line, a jingle repeated at 943 with decerpsi decerptaque. harundine is an ablative of instrument, the reed rod. mole is the same word as the moli he is leaning on at 916: he is propped against the kind of stonework he used to fish from.

sentences.t:
Sunt viridi prato confinia litora, quorum
altera pars undis, pars altera cingitur herbis,
quas neque cornigerae morsu laesere iuvencae,
nec placidae carpsistis oves hirtaeve capellae;
sentences.l: There are shores bordering on a green meadow, of which one part is ringed by waves, the other part by grasses, which no horn-bearing heifers have hurt with their biting, nor did you crop them, gentle sheep, or shaggy she-goats;
sentences.i: There is a stretch of shore running along a green meadow: one side of it is ringed by the sea, the other by grass — grass no horned heifer ever bit at, and you never grazed it either, quiet sheep, or you shaggy goats;
sentences.n: confinia is a neuter plural adjective taking the dative viridi prato, and litora is a poetic plural for one stretch of coast. 925 is chiastic: altera pars undis, pars altera … herbis, the two halves mirrored. laesere is laeserunt — the poetic third-person plural perfect in -ēre for -ērunt, which is easy to mistake for an infinitive; secuere at 930 is the same form. Then carpsistis swerves into the second person: mid-sentence the speaker turns aside from his account to address the sheep and the goats themselves, creatures who are in the scene only as the animals that never came.

sentences.l: no bee has carried flowers gathered from the seed away from there, no festive garlands have been given to a head, nor have sickle-bearing hands ever mown it;
sentences.i: no bee ever carried a flower off from it, no festive wreath was ever given to anyone's head, and no hand with a sickle in it ever cut it;
sentences.n: Three negatives in a row, non … non … neque umquam, build a single point: nothing living has ever touched this grass. conlectos semine is hard — the ablative semine with “gathered” has no easy sense, and the plainest reading is that the flowers came up from seed on their own. Magnus prints semine; the other witness reads sedula, which makes the phrase “no busy bee carried the gathered flowers off” and removes the difficulty altogether. genialia serta are garlands for a feast day; the Latin says only that no garland was ever given to a head, and leaves the reader to supply that any such garland would have been made from this grass. secuere is secuerunt, the same poetic perfect as laesere at 926.

sentences.t:
ego primus in illo
caespite consedi, dum lina madentia sicco,
sentences.l: I, the first, sat down on that turf, while I dry my dripping lines,
sentences.i: I was the first ever to sit on that turf, drying out my soaked lines,
sentences.n: primus is predicative: not “I sat down first” in some queue but “I was the first to sit there at all”, which is the whole point of the untouched grass described just before. dum keeps the present indicative sicco although consedi is perfect — Latin regularly holds the present for an action going on at the same time as a past one, and English has to shift it back to “while I was drying”.

sentences.t:
utque recenserem captivos ordine pisces,
insuper exposui, quos aut in retia casus
aut sua credulitas in aduncos egerat hamos.
sentences.l: and so that I might count over my captive fish in order, I laid them out on top, the ones which either chance had driven into the nets or their own trustfulness onto the curved hooks.
sentences.i: and so as to count my catch over one by one, I spread them out on it — fish that chance had driven into the nets, or their own gullibility onto the curved hooks.
sentences.n: ut … recenserem is a purpose clause. insuper is “on top”, that is, on the turf just described, and it is the detail the whole story turns on. The relative quos has two subjects sharing one pluperfect egerat, casus and sua credulitas, and the second is the fisherman's joke at his catch's expense: the net takes whatever comes, the hook takes the ones that believed it. captivos treats the fish as prisoners of war, which prepares dominum novum at 939.

sentences.t: Res similis fictae (sed quid mihi fingere prodest?):
sentences.l: The thing is like an invented one (but what does it profit me to invent?):
sentences.i: What comes next is like something made up — but what would I gain by making things up?
sentences.n: There is no verb in the first half: est has to be supplied, as it regularly is in a flat assertion of this kind. fictae is the perfect participle of fingo standing as a noun after similis, “like a made-up thing”; the form is both dative and genitive and similis governs either, so the case cannot be settled here; the parenthesis then re-uses the very same verb as an infinitive, fingere, so the whole disclaimer turns on one word used twice. mihi is a dative of the person concerned with prodest. Both the parenthesis and the colon are the edition's.

sentences.t:
gramine contacto coepit mea praeda moveri
et mutare latus terraque, ut in aequore, niti.
sentences.l: the grass once touched, my catch began to move and to change its side and to push itself on the land as in the sea.
sentences.i: The moment they touched the grass, my catch began to stir, to shift from one flank to the other, and to work along on dry land the way they do in water.
sentences.n: gramine contacto is another ablative absolute, like coetu soluto at 898 and versis membris at 905, and it carries the cause without ever saying “because”: the touching is what does it. praeda is singular, a collective “catch”, and the Latin keeps a singular verb, coepit, where English almost has to go plural. mutare latus is what a stranded fish does, turning from one flank to the other. niti takes the ablative terra, “to press against the ground”, and ut in aequore leaves its verb to be supplied from the clause before it.

sentences.t:
Dumque moror mirorque simul, fugit omnis in undas
turba suas dominumque novum litusque relinquunt.
sentences.l: And while I linger and marvel at the same time, the whole crowd flees into their own waves and they leave behind their new master and the shore.
sentences.i: And while I was still standing there wondering, the whole shoal made off into the water that was theirs and left their new owner, and the beach, behind.
sentences.n: moror and miror differ by a single letter, and the pairing makes his standing still and his amazement one act. dum again holds the present for a past action, as with sicco at 931. undas and its possessive suas are split by the line-end — undas closes 938, suas comes second in 939 with turba wedged between them — and the possessive is pointed: the waves are theirs, the shore and the fisherman are not. turba takes the singular fugit and then the plural relinquunt within one sentence, agreement first with the grammar and then with the sense. dominum novum is his own word for himself; he had owned them for a few minutes.

sentences.t:
Obstipui dubitoque diu causamque requiro,
num deus hoc aliquis, num sucus fecerit herbae.
sentences.l: I was stunned, and I hesitate a long while and I look for the cause: whether some god had done this, or the juice of the grass.
sentences.i: I was dumbfounded. I stood a long time uncertain, hunting for the cause — had some god done it, or the sap of the grass?
sentences.n: The perfect obstipui gives way to two presents, dubito and requiro, inside a single sentence: the historic present again, as with constitit and admiratur at 912–913. num … num sets out a double indirect question served by one verb, the perfect subjunctive fecerit. In 941 sucus is separated from its genitive herbae by that verb, so the line closes on the word that turns out to be the answer. deus aliquis, “some god or other”, is deliberately vague — he has no candidate in mind.

sentences.t:
“Quae” tamen “has” inquam “vires habet herba?”,manuque
pabula decerpsi decerptaque dente momordi.
sentences.l: “What grass,” though, I say, “has these powers?”, and with my hand I plucked the herbage and bit with my tooth what I had plucked.
sentences.i: “But what grass has power like this?” I said — and I picked the stuff with my hand and bit what I had picked.
sentences.n: The quoted question reaches the reader in three pieces: the edition prints Quae, then tamen, then has, then inquam, then vires habet herba, so that both the connective and the verb of speaking are pushed in among the words spoken. Read straight through, the question is Quae herba has vires habet? decerpsi decerptaque repeats the verb as its own participle, the same figure as ducebam ducentia at 922. One thing to flag about the archived edition: it prints herba?”,manuque, with the comma set hard against the closing quotation mark and no space at all before the next word. The sentence needs a space there; it is shipped exactly as the archive has it, unaltered.

sentences.t:
Vix bene combiberant ignotos guttura sucos,
cum subito trepidare intus praecordia sensi
alteriusque rapi naturae pectus amore,
sentences.l: Scarcely well had my throat drunk down the unknown juices, when suddenly I felt my inward parts shake within me and my breast snatched away by love of another nature,
sentences.i: My throat had barely swallowed that strange sap when I suddenly felt everything inside me shaking, and felt my heart dragged off by a longing for a different kind of being —
sentences.n: vix bene … cum subito is the inverted cum: the grammatical main clause is the one about the throat, while the event that matters sits in the cum-clause with an indicative verb, sensi. Two accusative-and-infinitive clauses hang from sensi — praecordia trepidare and pectus rapi — and the second is passive, so the heart is acted on rather than acting. alterius naturae is a genitive with amore: not desire for another creature but longing for another kind of existence. guttura is a poetic plural for one throat, as pectora will be at 953.

sentences.t:
nec potui restare diu “repetenda” que “numquam
terra, vale!” dixi corpusque sub aequora mersi.
sentences.l: nor could I stay long, and “never again to be sought — land, farewell!” I said, and I plunged my body beneath the waters.
sentences.i: I could not stay above long. “Land I shall never come back for — goodbye!” I said, and drove my body down under the sea.
sentences.n: repetenda is a gerundive agreeing with the vocative terra: “land that is never to be sought again”. The gerundive carries necessity, and that is what makes the farewell final — he is not deciding against a return, he is telling the land it cannot be returned to. The edition sets the enclitic que outside the closing quotation mark, between “repetenda” and “numquam”, so once more the quoted words are broken around something that is not part of them, as at 918 and 942. mersi is transitive here, with corpus its object: he sinks his own body rather than being sunk.

sentences.t:
Di maris exceptum socio dignantur honore,
utque mihi quaecumque feram mortalia, demant,
Oceanum Tethynque rogant:
sentences.l: The gods of the sea deem me, taken in, worthy of a fellow's honour, and they ask Ocean and Tethys to take away from me whatever mortal things I bear:
sentences.i: The sea-gods took me in and judged me worth a colleague's honour, and they asked Ocean and Tethys to strip away from me whatever was still mortal in me:
sentences.n: exceptum is a perfect passive participle, “received, taken in”, and the me it agrees with is never written; that same unexpressed me is the object of dignantur, so Latin packs “they took me in and judged me worthy” into one clause. dignantur is deponent and takes the ablative honore. socius honos is the honour due to a partner, not to a superior, and it repeats in the sea-gods' own act the equal ius he claimed for himself at 918–919. ut … demant is an indirect command after rogant; mihi is a dative of separation, “take away from me”; and feram is subjunctive because its clause sits inside that command.

sentences.l: I am purified by them, and, a spell that purges wrong having been spoken over me nine times, I am ordered to put my breast under a hundred rivers;
sentences.i: They purified me; a charm that washes pollution away was said over me nine times, and then I was told to hold my chest under a hundred rivers;
sentences.n: Both verbs are passive, lustror and iubeor: the rite is done to him and he performs none of it himself. carmine dicto is another ablative absolute, with purgante nefas hung on carmine — “the song, purging wrong”. nefas is religious pollution, the state of being unfit to come near the gods, not a crime with a penalty attached. noviens, nine times, is a ritual count. iubeo in the passive keeps its infinitive, so iubeor supponere is “I am ordered to place”. In 953 fluminibus and its numeral centum are pulled apart, with iubeor supponere standing between them.

sentences.t:
nec mora, diversis lapsi de partibus amnes
totaque vertuntur supra caput aequora nostrum.
sentences.l: and no delay: rivers, having glided down from different quarters, and whole seas are turned over our head.
sentences.i: No delay: rivers came sliding down from every direction, and whole seas were tipped over my head.
sentences.n: nec mora is a verbless formula, “and there was no waiting”. lapsi is the perfect participle of the deponent labor and is therefore active in sense — “having glided”, not “having been let slip” — the same point as nacta at 902. nostrum is the poetic plural for “my”: there is one head under all that water. tota aequora, “whole seas”, answers the hundred rivers of 953 by outbidding them. In 955 tota is separated from aequora by three words, and caput from nostrum by aequora.

sentences.t:
Hactenus acta tibi possum memoranda referre,
hactenus haec memini, nec mens mea cetera sensit.
sentences.l: Thus far I can report to you deeds worth recording, thus far I remember these things, and my mind did not perceive the rest.
sentences.i: That is as far as I can tell you anything worth telling; that is as far as my memory reaches — my mind took in nothing after that.
sentences.n: The doubled hactenus marks the seam of the story, and the second use narrows the first: what is worth telling, then what he can remember at all. memoranda is a gerundive doing an adjective's work — “deeds that must be recorded”, hence “worth the telling”. tibi is Scylla, whom he has been addressing since virgo at 917. The admission does real work: the change itself happened while he was not conscious, which is why what comes next is the description of a body he found already made.

sentences.t:
Quae postquam rediit, alium me corpore toto
ac fueram nuper, neque eundem mente recepi.
sentences.l: And when it came back, I took myself back as another in my whole body than I had lately been, and not the same in mind.
sentences.i: When it came back, I took myself back as somebody else in body — nothing like what I had been a moment before — and not the same in mind either.
sentences.n: Quae is a connecting relative: a relative pronoun opening a new sentence where English wants a plain pronoun, “and it”, reaching back to mens in 957. alium … ac fueram is the comparative “other than I had been”, with ac introducing the second term instead of quam. corpore and mente are ablatives of respect, “as to body”, “as to mind”. recepi is the verb for getting back what is your own — he recovers himself and finds a stranger in his hands.

sentences.t:
Hanc ego tum primum viridem ferrugine barbam
caesariemque meam, quam longa per aequora verro,
ingentesque umeros et caerula bracchia vidi
cruraque pinnigero curvata novissima pisce.
sentences.l: Then for the first time I saw this beard of mine, green with iron-rust, and my hair, which I sweep across the long waters, and huge shoulders and sea-blue arms, and legs curved at their furthest ends into a finned fish.
sentences.i: That was the first time I saw this beard of mine, green as tarnished iron, and this hair I trail across the open sea, and the huge shoulders, the dark-blue arms, and the legs that run out curved into a finned fish.
sentences.n: The verb vidi is withheld to the very end of 962: four accusative objects pile up ahead of it — barbam, caesariem, umeros, bracchia — and a fifth, crura, follows it in 963; the literal has to bring the verb forward to stay readable. ferrugine is the colour of iron rust, used in Latin of a dark blue-green, and caerula in 962 is the same range of colour. hanc barbam, caesariem meam and the present tense of verro plant the description in front of Scylla: he is pointing at himself as he speaks. caesariem is the very word for what she was staring at in 914, now named by its owner. novissima is “furthest, last”, agreeing with crura, and pinnigero pisce is the ablative into which they curve.

sentences.t:
Quid tamen haec species, quid dis placuisse marinis,
quid iuvat esse deum, si tu non tangeris istis?”
sentences.l: But what does this form avail, what to have pleased the sea-gods, what to be a god, if you are not touched by these things?”
sentences.i: But what use is this shape, what use is it to have won over the gods of the sea, what use is it to be a god at all, if none of it touches you?”
sentences.n: One verb, iuvat, carries all three questions, and quid is repeated three times — at the head of 964, again inside 964 after its first clause, and at the head of 965. haec species is the subject of the first; the infinitives placuisse and esse deum serve as subjects of the other two. istis is the demonstrative of the second person, “those things of yours”, meaning here “all this, as it bears on you”. tangeris is passive, so the speech closes with Scylla as the one who is to be moved rather than the one who moves; the very last word is istis, the things that were supposed to move her. It is a complaint rather than a question, and the whole account has been built to reach it.

sentences.t:
Talia dicentem, dicturum plura, reliquit
Scylla deum;
sentences.l: Him speaking such things, about to speak more, Scylla left — the god;
sentences.i: He was still speaking, with more to say, when Scylla walked off and left the god there;
sentences.n: dicentem (present) and dicturum (future) are both accusative participles agreeing with deum, and they set what he is doing against what he will not get to do. The noun they modify is held back to the second word of 967, after the subject Scylla has arrived. reliquit is the plain verb for leaving a thing behind. She gives no answer, and there is no speech from her anywhere in these lines.

sentences.t:
furit ille inritatusque repulsa
prodigiosa petit Titanidos atria Circes.
sentences.l: he rages, and, provoked by the rebuff, he seeks the portent-filled halls of Circe the Titan's daughter.
sentences.i: He is in a fury; stung by the refusal, he makes for the monstrous halls of Circe, the Titan's daughter.
sentences.n: furit and petit are both present, and the two of them carry the close. repulsa is a noun here, “a rebuff”, in the ablative of cause with inritatus — not the participle of repello. prodigiosa answers prodigium at 917: he told Scylla he was no prodigium, and the moment she leaves he goes off to a house full of them. Titanidos and Circes both keep their Greek genitive endings in the edition rather than being Latinised. The part ends on the doorway of a place it does not enter.
